articles.title: AlphaGenome 2: How Google DeepMind Taught an AI to Read DNA Through a Cell's Eyes
articles.excerpt: AlphaGenome 2: How Google DeepMind Taught an AI to Read DNA Through a Cell's Eyes For decades, one of the hardest problems in human genetics has been connecting a DNA variant to the specific cell type…
articles.body: AlphaGenome 2: How Google DeepMind Taught an AI to Read DNA Through a Cell's Eyes For decades, one of the hardest problems in human genetics has been connecting a DNA variant to the specific cell type where it actually does something. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) can flag thousands of variants linked to disease, but most of them sit in non-coding regions — the 98% of the genome that doesn't encode proteins — and their effects depend entirely on which cell is reading that stretch of DNA. A variant that disrupts gene regulation in a gut immune cell may be invisible in a liver cell. Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 , announced on November 11, 2026, is a direct attempt to solve this problem.

articles.title: System Design, Plainly — Part 9: Database Indexes
articles.excerpt: On a Tuesday morning, a team shipped a feature that let users search their own order history. The query was one line — WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 — and it ran in 3 millisecond…
articles.body: On a Tuesday morning, a team shipped a feature that let users search their own order history. The query was one line — WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 — and it ran in 3 milliseconds in staging. In production, with 100 million orders, it ran in 5 seconds. Same query, same code, same database. The difference was 100 million rows and one missing line in the schema: there was no index on user_id , so every search read every order ever placed, sorted them, and threw away all but twenty. The fix was also one line — CREATE INDEX — and the query went back to 0.32 milliseconds. Not 5 seconds to 4 seconds. Five seconds to a third of a millisecond: a 15,625x speedup from a single line of DDL.

articles.title: Stopping a memory dump from recovering your assembly
articles.excerpt: Rename every type, encrypt every string, flatten every branch — and an attacker can skip all of it with one move: let your program start, then copy the assembly straight out of its own memory and open…
articles.body: Rename every type, encrypt every string, flatten every branch — and an attacker can skip all of it with one move: let your program start, then copy the assembly straight out of its own memory and open that in a decompiler. The runtime has already done the hard part. Strings are decrypted on first use, metadata is resolved, the JIT has the real tokens. A process dump captures a module that is, in some ways, cleaner than the file you shipped. This is the attack obfuscation alone does nothing about, and the countermeasure — anti-dump — is one of the more misunderstood protections in the box. Here's exactly what a dumper relies on, how Nebula.NET takes it away, and where the technique stops. What a dumper actually does A managed assembly is a PE file.

articles.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
articles.excerpt: The Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 17-18, sending shooting stars racing across the night sky from the direction of the constellation Leo.
articles.body: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!

articles.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
articles.excerpt: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send message…
articles.body: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment.

articles.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
articles.excerpt: The legend of the Black Knight satellite offers an example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can accumulate into a single conspiracy theory over time.
articles.body: In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction.

articles.title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
articles.excerpt: Sierra Space's Dream Chaser is aiming for its first spaceflight after more than 20 years of development, and the space plane now has FAA approval to come home.
articles.body: The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut. Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9). The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated .
